newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China, Taiwan, HK stocks end higher on confidence.
newsitem.headline: China, Taiwan, HK stocks end higher on confidence.

text.p: Stocks in Hong Kong, China and Taiwan closed higher on Friday, supported by growing confidence for a smooth transition of power in Beijing following the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
"People are more confident about market sentiment after the death of Mr Deng," said Henry Lui, research analyst at Mansion House Research in Hong Kong.
"They seem to think that the political situation in China will be very stable and that is why they look back to the fundamentals of local blue chips," he said.
After a bout of profit-taking early in the session, buyers returned and drove the Hang Seng Index up 33.52 points, or 0.25 percent, to 13,444.85 at the close.
Market strategists believe the next major hurdle for the markets will be China's 15th Party Congress, which takes place in October.
If there are to be any challenges to the current leadership, they will occur then and not before or immediately after June 30, when Hong Kong reverts to China, they said.
"The next real big hurdle will be the Party Congress," one strategist said.
Shares on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges also closed higher on Friday on buying by both retail investors and institutions, brokers said.
Brokers said a decision by securities houses in Shanghai to keep markets stable without intervening to support them aided sentiment.
Shanghai's foreign-currency B share index was up 0.894 points, or 1.38 percent, to 65.569, while domestic A shares rose 55.545 points, or 5.51 percent, to a high for the year of 1,063.276.
Shenzhen's B share index was up 7.43 points, or 5.18 percent at 150.96, while the A share index rose 8.68 points, or 2.48 percent, to 359.28.
Taiwan stocks rallied to a six-year high after the government late on Thursday announced gross domestic product for the fourth quarter of 1996 was 6.62 percent, above an expected 6.58 percent.
The weighted index shrugged off Deng's death to climb 113.15 points or 1.47 percent to end at 7,791.19. It was the highest close since June 2, 1990, when the index ended at 7,857.01.
Singapore stocks fell on profit-taking ahead of the upcoming corporate results season in March, with the Straits Times Index down 10.70 points, or 0.48 percent, at 2,241.28.
In other Asian markets, trading had been mixed early in the session following a 92-point drop in Wall Street.
Tokyo stocks forfeited early gains to end slightly lower after trading in a narrow range. The key Nikkei 225-share index was off 17.17 points, or 0.09 percent, at 19,034.54.
Philippine shares were off 2.17 points, or 0.26 percent, at 3,301.98, while Indonesian shares lost 2.17 points, or 0.31 percent, to 696.50.
Shares in Seoul were off 24.41 points, or 3.43 percent, at 686.72. Concern over rising interest rates dampened sentiment.
Australian stocks lost 1.0 point, or 0.04 percent, to 2,475.3, while New Zealand shares were down 24.32 points, or 1.05 percent, at 2,301.53.

The dollar recovered slightly from overnight losses but the near-term direction was unclear. In late Tokyo trade, the U.S. currency was quoted at around 122.85 yen, compared with 122.55 at the close in New York and at 1.6857 marks against 1.6863.
